chief_complaint: coughing up cupfuls of thick foul-smelling yellow phlegm daily and recurrent chest infections for 4 years
hpi_details: 4-year history of a daily, chronic, productive cough producing large volumes (up to a half-cup / 100 mL daily) of thick, tenacious, foul-smelling purulent green/yellow sputum. Accompanied by intermittent blood streaking in the phlegm, chronic breathlessness when carrying groceries, and severe fatigue. Suffers from recurrent lower respiratory tract infections requiring courses of oral antibiotics at least 4 to 5 times every winter. Had a severe, prolonged episode of whooping cough (Bordetella pertussis) and complicated pneumonia during childhood at age 7. Denies smoking cigarettes or acid reflux.
ideas: thinks the severe childhood pneumonia damaged her lung tubes causing pockets where pus collects and festers
concerns: embarrassed by the constant foul-smelling coughing in public and worried about coughing up larger amounts of blood
expectations: wants specialized chest physiotherapy instruction, daily mucous-clearing inhalers, and long-term antibiotics to stop the recurrent infections
pmh: childhood severe pertussis/pneumonia at age 7, recurrent bronchitis
medications: amoxicillin 500mg TDS during frequent acute flare-ups
social_hx: never smoked, zero alcohol, retired librarian, lives with husband

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Bronchiectasis is essential for appropriate diagnostic workup and treatment.
Clinical history, severity assessment, and targeted testing must be interpreted together rather than relying on one symptom alone.
Teach and support regular airway-clearance physiotherapy.
Management should follow local pathways and account for patient-specific comorbidity and clinical severity.

common_misconceptions: Assuming a mild or atypical presentation rules out Bronchiectasis.
Relying on a single normal test result to prematurely exclude serious pathology.
Equating transient symptom improvement with resolution of the underlying condition.
Failing to consider clinically important alternative diagnoses.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before appropriate assessment.
Starting treatment without considering contraindications, interactions, or organ function.
Ignoring critical warning signs: Massive haemoptysis.
management_principles: Teach and support regular airway-clearance physiotherapy.
Send sputum cultures during exacerbations and use culture-directed antibiotics.
Arrange HRCT confirmation and investigate treatable causes, including ABPA and immunodeficiency.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 63F non-smoker with childhood pneumonia history presents with 4-year daily high-volume purulent sputum production (>100mL/day), haemoptysis, and 5x/year infective exacerbations.
reference_soap.objective: Perform targeted physical examination. Inspection: examine fingers demonstrating bilateral finger clubbing. Auscultation: coarse, low-pitched, bubbling inspiratory and expiratory crackles ('popping' sounds) heard over both lower lobes, accompanied by scattered wheezes that characteristically shift or clear partially after vigorous coughing and expectoration. Sputum microbiology: send routine and persistent sputum cultures -> confirms chronic colonization with Pseudomonas aeruginosa (or Haemophilus influenzae). High-Resolution CT (HRCT) Chest (thin-section 1mm slices -> gold standard diagnostic test): demonstrates definitive Bronchiectasis -> permanent, abnormal dilatation of the bronchi with internal broncho-arterial ratio >1.0 ('signet-ring sign' where the dilated bronchus is larger than its accompanying pulmonary artery), lack of normal bronchial tapering toward the periphery, and thickened bronchial walls ('tram-track sign').
reference_soap.assessment: Non-Cystic Fibrosis (Non-CF) Post-Infectious Bronchiectasis complicated by chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa airway colonization. DDx: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD -> occurs in smokers without signet-ring sign or daily high-volume purulent sputum), Cystic Fibrosis (check sweat chloride test / CFTR gene mutation in younger patients), Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis (ABPA -> check total IgE / Aspergillus precipitins), primary ciliary dyskinesia, immunoglobulin deficiency (check IgG/IgA/IgM levels).
reference_soap.plan: Primary cornerstone of management: daily airway-clearance physiotherapy (refer to a respiratory physiotherapist for instruction in Active Cycle of Breathing Techniques, postural drainage, and an oscillating positive expiratory pressure device). Consider a mucoactive treatment only after clinician review of tolerance and contraindications. During exacerbations, obtain sputum cultures and use clinician-directed, culture-guided antibiotics. If chronic Pseudomonas colonization or frequent exacerbations are confirmed, a respiratory specialist may consider inhaled antipseudomonal antibiotics or long-term macrolide therapy after appropriate ECG, mycobacterial testing, interaction review, and monitoring. Escalate urgently for massive haemoptysis, hypoxaemia, or severe breathlessness.

learning_objectives: Identify the pathognomonic HRCT signs of Bronchiectasis: signet-ring sign (broncho-arterial ratio >1.0), lack of tapering, and tram-track sign
Correlate daily high-volume purulent expectoration (>100mL/day) and digital clubbing with permanent post-infectious bronchial dilation
Explain how respiratory-physiotherapist-taught Active Cycle of Breathing Techniques can support airway clearance
Recognize when respiratory-specialist review is needed to consider long-term inhaled antibiotics or macrolide therapy

teaching.one_liner: Chronic productive cough with recurrent infections, high-volume purulent sputum, and HRCT evidence of permanently dilated bronchi.

history.answer: I've been coughing up nearly half a cup of thick, foul-smelling yellow-green phlegm every single day, and I keep getting chest infections.
This daily heavy coughing has been going on continuously for the past four years.
It started gradually after a particularly bad chest cold four years ago, but I've always had vulnerable lungs since childhood.
I bring up thick, sticky greenish-yellow phlegm every day, roughly half a cup, and it has an awful rotten smell.
It is worst in the morning when I first wake up and when I lie flat on my back, as the mucus seems to pool inside my chest.
I don't have sudden choking attacks, whooping gasps, or vomiting after coughing; it is just a relentless, heavy productive cough.
Cold winter air and brisk walking definitely make me cough harder and bring up even more mucus.
I feel chest tightness and hear rattling or wheezing sounds, and I get breathless simply carrying groceries up the front steps.
I don't have a fever or chills right now, though I spike high fevers whenever an acute chest infection sets in.
Yes, every few weeks I notice thin streaks of bright red blood mixed into the phlegm, but never large mouthfuls of pure blood.
I haven't lost any noticeable weight, and I don't suffer from drenching night sweats.
My chest feels tight and achy from coughing all day, but I don't have sharp, stabbing pain when taking a deep breath.
No, I don't have a runny nose, nasal blockage, or mucus dripping down the back of my throat.
No heartburn, sour fluid backing up into my mouth, or throat irritation after meals.
I don't need extra pillows to breathe at night, and my feet and ankles never swell up.
I do not take any blood pressure pills or ACE inhibitors.
Every winter I come down with four or five severe chest infections that require courses of antibiotics from my doctor.
When I was seven years old, I had a very severe bout of whooping cough that turned into complicated pneumonia, keeping me sick for months.
No, I never had chronic sinus problems, childhood digestive trouble, greasy stools, or frequent skin and ear infections.
history.topic: Immune deficiency and cystic fibrosis screening

history.answer: Apart from the severe childhood pneumonia and repeated winter chest infections, I have no other chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and have not been hospitalized since that severe pneumonia episode when I was seven.
I only take amoxicillin tablets three times a day whenever my chest flares up with an infection; I take no regular daily prescriptions.
I don't have any known allergies to medications, foods, or environmental triggers.
I have never smoked a single cigarette in my life.
I don't drink any alcohol at all.
I am a retired librarian and live comfortably with my husband in a quiet, dry home.
No history of mold, chemical fumes, heavy dust, or pet birds at home or at my past workplace.
No, I have never had tuberculosis, and to my knowledge I have never been exposed to anyone who had it.
No one in my house or close circle is currently sick or coughing.
There is no family history of cystic fibrosis, early lung disease, or chronic respiratory infections.
No history of asthma, allergic rhinitis, or childhood eczema.
I went through menopause over ten years ago, so there is no chance of pregnancy.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, pulse 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air.
Bilateral finger clubbing is present on the digits; no peripheral cyanosis.
Nasal mucosa is pink without polyps or purulence; posterior pharynx is clear without erythema or cobblestoning.
No palpable cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Symmetrical chest expansion without intercostal indrawing or localized tenderness.
Resonant to percussion throughout all lung fields bilaterally.
Coarse bubbling inspiratory and expiratory crackles with scattered wheezes over bilateral lower lung bases, which partially clear after coughing.
Normal S1 and S2 with regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
No pitting edema over either lower extremity.
